nameStory: The pellucid glass-snail gets its name from its remarkably transparent shell that you can practically see through, like looking through a window. "Pellucid" comes from the Latin word meaning "transparent" or "clear," while "glass snail" refers to the shell's crystal-clear, glassy appearance that sets it apart from most other snails.
description: The pellucid glass-snail is a tiny terrestrial snail with an incredibly thin, nearly transparent shell that looks like it's made of delicate glass. These miniature land snails are among the smallest you'll encounter, typically measuring less than half an inch across. Their shells are so clear that you can often see the snail's soft body parts right through the shell walls, giving them an almost ethereal appearance as they glide across moist surfaces.

idTips.label: Transparent Shell
idTips.description: The shell is remarkably clear and glassy, almost like looking through a soap bubble - you can see the snail's body and organs through the shell walls

idTips.label: Tiny Size
idTips.description: Extremely small, typically less than half an inch across - about the size of a small pea or your pinky fingernail

idTips.label: Fragile Feel
idTips.description: The shell feels incredibly delicate and thin to the touch, like it might crack if you breathe on it too hard

idTips.label: Low, Flattened Shape
idTips.description: Shell is relatively flat and low-spiraled rather than tall and pointed, with a wide opening

idTips.label: Glossy Surface
idTips.description: Shell surface is smooth and glossy when wet, catching light like a tiny crystal

habitat: Look for pellucid glass-snails in very moist, shaded areas like under logs, leaf litter, or moss in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England. They prefer spots that stay consistently damp, such as near streams, in ravines, or under thick canopy cover where the soil rarely dries out completely.

seasonality.spring: Most active as temperatures warm and moisture increases from snowmelt and spring rains. Look under newly fallen logs and in fresh leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Active during humid periods and after rain showers, but may retreat deeper into cover during dry spells to avoid desiccation.
seasonality.fall: Can be found actively feeding on decomposing leaves and fungi as they prepare for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Dormant and hidden deep in soil, under logs, or in protected crevices - rarely observed during cold months.

funFact: These snails are so transparent that scientists can actually watch their hearts beating and observe their digestive systems working in real-time without harming the animal - like having a living, breathing anatomical model!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other tiny land snails, but the pellucid glass-snail's see-through shell is unmistakable once you know what to look for. Remember: if you can see through it like glass, you've found your pellucid glass-snail!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "glass snails," these creatures are actually quite hardy and well-adapted to their environment - the transparent shell isn't a sign of weakness but rather an evolutionary adaptation that may help with camouflage or temperature regulation.
compareHints: Since this is the only Vitrina species commonly found in New England, compare it to other small land snails in the region. Unlike most land snails with opaque, colored shells, the pellucid glass-snail's transparent shell makes it instantly recognizable. Other tiny snails like amber snails may be small and glossy, but they lack the crystal-clear transparency that makes glass snails so distinctive.
